rows.geometry_precision: archaeological settlement/site extent; modern heritage boundary is only a display proxy
rows.bounded_conclusion: Cahokia's Mound 72 provides strong evidence of hierarchical violence and ritual sacrifice. Some scholarship interprets sacrificed low-status individuals as enslaved, but bioarchaeological work undermines older assumptions that key mass-burial groups were non-local captives; slave status is therefore not securely established for the site at c.1200.
rows.required_abstention: Do not convert sacrifice, poor health, hierarchy, or presumed foreign origin into a slavery-status claim; do not generalize Mound 72 to citywide prevalence.
rows.unresolved_reason: Whether particular Mound 72 individuals were enslaved remains interpretively disputed; the archaeological evidence establishes sacrifice more securely than legal/social slave status.

rows.geometry_precision: Kilwa island/urban locus; not the whole Swahili coast
rows.bounded_conclusion: Near-anchor written and archaeological scholarship supports the presence of enslaved people in the Kilwa urban/archipelago context and a longer Swahili-coast history of slaving. The scale and exact mechanics of slave trading at Kilwa around 1400 remain poorly resolved.
rows.required_abstention: Do not infer that all Swahili-coast urban life or trade was slave-based, and do not treat proposed holding/market structures as proven slave-market facilities.
rows.network_territorial_warning: Kilwa's Indian Ocean connectivity and evidence of enslaved people are network/site claims; they do not establish territorial prevalence along the wider Swahili coast.
rows.evidence_locus_type: port-city / island / nearby archipelago archaeology and written travel context
rows.unresolved_reason: Pre-sixteenth-century scale and local prevalence are not quantifiable from the bounded evidence; some archaeological slave-market interpretations remain tentative.

rows.geometry_precision: Cluny institutional locus plus documented dependent properties; no single bounded territorial jurisdiction
rows.bounded_conclusion: Cluniac charters around the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries directly record persons designated servi and ancillae being donated to, attached to, or becoming property/dependents of Cluniac churches and monks. This securely supports institutional unfree servile dependency around 1100.
rows.required_abstention: Do not automatically translate every medieval servus/ancilla as chattel slave, and do not infer a single prevalence rate or uniform status across all Cluniac lands.
rows.law_practice_note: Charters document formal transfers/status relations; they do not by themselves recover lived conditions or a uniform legal category across all estates.
rows.evidence_locus_type: institutional charters and dependent church/estate relationships
rows.unresolved_reason: Terminological boundary between slavery, serfdom, and other hereditary servile dependence requires contextual interpretation.

rows.geometry_precision: institutional locus in Fatimid Cairo only
rows.bounded_conclusion: Slavery was deeply embedded in Fatimid and eleventh–twelfth-century Cairo, but the bounded packet does not establish slave ownership, slave labour, or a slavery institution specifically within al-Azhar at c.1100.
rows.required_abstention: Do not infer al-Azhar institutional slaveholding from slavery in Fatimid armies, Cairo households, markets, or from the fact that al-Azhar was founded by the Fatimid conqueror Jawhar.
rows.network_territorial_warning: Cairo-wide slave markets and imperial slave recruitment are contextual layers, not al-Azhar institutional practice.
rows.evidence_locus_type: institutional point within a slaveholding urban/imperial context
rows.unresolved_reason: No target-specific al-Azhar ownership/labour evidence was established within the bounded packet.

rows.access_language_warning: Geniza-based Cairo evidence is rich but does not automatically identify al-Azhar as slaveholding.

rows.geometry_precision: schematic changing network of corridors and hubs; no single fixed line
rows.bounded_conclusion: Sixth- and seventh-century Turfan evidence documents Sogdian and other merchants buying, selling, and travelling with enslaved people on an identifiable Silk Road segment, supporting slavery/slave-trade participation in the network around the 700 anchor.
rows.required_abstention: Do not paint the whole Silk Road as a slave-trading territory or infer equal incidence along every corridor; the evidence is concentrated in specific hubs, documents, and travelers.
rows.law_practice_note: Tang legal restrictions on enslaving free imperial subjects may have shaped demand for foreign enslaved people, but this is not a network-wide legal regime.
rows.network_territorial_warning: This is explicitly a route/network participation claim, not territorial practice for every polity crossed by the network.
rows.evidence_locus_type: Turfan oasis documents and transregional traveler/merchant network
rows.unresolved_reason: The network has no singular boundary or uniform practice; quantitative claims from small Turfan document samples cannot be generalized network-wide.

rows.geometry_precision: schematic maritime/river/trading network varying by decade
rows.bounded_conclusion: Ninth-century and broader Viking-Age evidence supports captive-taking, enslavement, transport, and sale as recurring components of Viking raiding and trading networks, including Dublin, Birka, Hedeby and related routes.
rows.required_abstention: Do not treat 'Vikings' as one territorial society, infer uniform household slavery across all Scandinavian regions, or map every Viking route as equally involved in slave trading.
rows.network_territorial_warning: The strongest claim is network/activity participation; individual port and territorial practice require separate evidence.
rows.evidence_locus_type: mobile raiding/trading networks and documented market nodes
rows.unresolved_reason: The archaeology of sale/holding spaces is often indirect and the network has no single territorial boundary.

rows.geometry_precision: archipelago/community frame; historical community boundaries are not a single resolved polygon
rows.bounded_conclusion: Later ethnographic writing preserves a Samoan category of conquered people (tangata taua) whose condition was described as little better than slavery, while twentieth-century comparative coding records 'absence of slavery.' These retrospective sources do not securely resolve the institution or its prevalence at c.1700.
rows.required_abstention: Do not back-project nineteenth- or twentieth-century ethnographic classification unchanged to 1700, and do not equate chiefly/kin obligations, conquered status, or later plantation indenture with one slavery category.
rows.evidence_locus_type: retrospective ethnographic descriptions across Samoan communities
rows.unresolved_reason: The accessible evidence is retrospective and internally difficult to reconcile; target-year institutional continuity is not established.

sources.title: Old Samoa, or, Flotsam and Jetsam from the Pacific Ocean
sources.author: John B. Stair

rows.access_language_warning: Both principal classifications are much later than 1700; oral history and Samoan-language scholarship are underrepresented.

rows.geometry_precision: island-group/community frame containing multiple distinct peoples; no single indigenous polity
rows.bounded_conclusion: British activity in the Andamans from the late eighteenth century included the kidnapping and confinement of indigenous islanders; this supports a bounded external-colonial captivity/coercion claim around the 1800 anchor.
rows.required_abstention: Do not convert British kidnapping/confinement into evidence that Andamanese communities practiced internal slavery, and do not collapse multiple island peoples into one society.
rows.law_practice_note: Colonial capture/confinement is an external coercive relation, not an indigenous legal regime.
rows.network_territorial_warning: The evidence concerns colonial encounters and captured individuals rather than island-wide territorial practice.
rows.evidence_locus_type: colonial encounter across specific island/coastal contacts
rows.unresolved_reason: Internal community slavery/status at 1800 remains unassessed; the supported claim is external British captivity.

sources.title: Colonization, kidnap and confinement in the Andamans penal colony, 1771–1864
sources.author: Clare Anderson

rows.access_language_warning: Colonial documentation dominates the accessible record; indigenous perspectives and distinct community histories are unevenly preserved.

gate.note: All eight researched cases are representable as site, institution, network, or fuzzy-community claims while territorial inference remains explicitly prohibited.
